identification.summary: Mandiant describes UNC1860 as a persistent and opportunistic Iranian state-sponsored threat actor that is likely affiliated with Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) [S1]. Mandiant assesses it is a probable initial access provider that holds persistent access to high-priority government and telecommunications networks in the Middle East and hands access to other actors, including MOIS-affiliated APT34 [S1]. Its specialized tooling includes GUI-operated controllers (TEMPLEPLAY, VIROGREEN) and passive backdoors with no outbound C2 [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Mandiant's report (2024-09-19) describes overlaps with Albania-related activity in 2022 and an engagement in 2020 in which UNC1860 staged scanning from a victim network; it gives no single first-seen date for the cluster [S1]. Related cluster DEV-0861 (Microsoft) began mail exfiltration in April 2020 and exploited SharePoint in May 2021 [S2].
identification.notes: UNC1860 is Mandiant's uncategorized-cluster name [S1]. Mandiant states that Shrouded Snooper (Cisco Talos), Scarred Manticore (Check Point) and Storm-0861 (Microsoft) share tradecraft and targeting with UNC1860 [S1]; this is an overlap statement, not a stated one-to-one equivalence, so facts from those clusters are kept separate here. Microsoft's 2022 post uses the temporary name DEV-0861, which Microsoft says maps to Storm-0861 under its April 2023 naming update, and links DEV-0861 with moderate confidence to EUROPIUM (later Hazel Sandstorm) [S2]. Check Point equates Scarred Manticore with Storm-0861 [S5]. Talos reported ShroudedSnooper in September 2023 with no attribution to a known group [S4]. No Microsoft Threat Intelligence report naming UNC1860 directly was found.

attribution.sponsor: Iran, with Mandiant assessing a likely affiliation with the Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) [S1].
attribution.confidence: Mandiant states the MOIS affiliation as 'likely' [S1]. For the related DEV-0861 cluster, Microsoft assessed Iranian government affiliation and linked it with moderate confidence to EUROPIUM [S2]. Check Point says Scarred Manticore is MOIS-affiliated [S3]. Mandiant says it could not independently corroborate UNC1860's role in the 2022 Albania or 2023 Israel destructive operations [S1].
attribution.basis: Mandiant: tooling overlaps and hand-off tooling, targeting, and victim overlap with suspected APT34 intrusions in 2019-2020 [S1]. Microsoft: victimology and tool links to MOIS-associated actors for DEV-0861 [S2]. Check Point: victim overlap and hand-off of targets between Scarred Manticore and Void Manticore [S5]. These are vendor assessments; no government attribution of UNC1860 was found.

objectives: Mandiant assesses UNC1860's role is to gain and maintain persistent access to high-priority networks, particularly government and telecommunications in the Middle East, and to pass that access to other Iranian actors; it does not state an end-state objective for the cluster itself [S1].

regions: Saudi Arabia and Qatar (2020 engagement: Saudi IP space scanned, Saudi and Qatari domain credentials validated) [S1]
Albania and Israel (related-cluster destructive operations; UNC1860 role not corroborated) [S1]
DEV-0861 victim profile: Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, UAE [S2]
targeting.notes: Mandiant says UNC1860 opportunistically exploits internet-facing servers [S1]. Check Point reports Scarred Manticore also targeting military, IT providers, financial organizations and NGOs in the Middle East; this is a separate cluster and is not attributed to UNC1860 [S3].

capabilities.summary: Initial access is via opportunistic exploitation of internet-facing servers followed by web shell deployment; Mandiant names SharePoint CVE-2019-0604, exploited by the VIROGREEN framework [S1]. Web shell and dropper tooling: STAYSHANTE web shell and SASHEYAWAY dropper (embeds passive backdoors TEMPLEDOOR, FACEFACE, SPARKLOAD) [S1]. GUI controllers TEMPLEPLAY (for TEMPLEDOOR; command execution, file transfer, HTTP proxy for RDP to hosts behind NAT/firewalls) and VIROGREEN could let third-party operators with no prior knowledge of a target access networks and deploy payloads [S1]. Passive implants include OATBOAT, the WINTAPIX kernel driver (code similar to TOFUDRV), TOFUDRV/TOFULOAD using undocumented IOCTLs, and TEMPLEDROP, which repurposes a legitimate Iranian AV file-system filter driver (Sheed AV) to protect its files [S1]. Other tools: TEMPLELOCK (Event Log service interference), TUNNELBOI (tunneling and RDP setup) [S1]. Passive implants make no outbound C2; commands may arrive from VPN nodes in the target country, other victims or internal hosts [S1]. Mandiant notes kernel drivers are high risk, high reward, giving lower detection rates [S1]. Related cluster tooling: LIONTAIL memory-resident framework using HTTP.sys (Scarred Manticore) [S3] and HTTPSnoop/PipeSnoop impersonating Cortex XDR components (ShroudedSnooper) [S4].

campaigns.name: Overlap with suspected APT34 victims
campaigns.summary: Mandiant observed organizations compromised by suspected APT34 as earlier compromised by UNC1860, and vice versa, which it reads as a support role for lateral movement.

campaigns.name: Staging engagement against Saudi and Qatari targets
campaigns.summary: UNC1860 used a victim network as a staging area, scanned mostly Saudi IP space for exposed vulnerabilities, validated credentials for Qatari and Saudi domains, and targeted regional VPN servers.

campaigns.name: DEV-0861 intrusion into Albanian government (related cluster)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reports DEV-0861 began mail exfiltration from organizations in several countries in April 2020, exploited CVE-2019-0604 on an unpatched SharePoint server in May 2021 and implanted web shells, and exfiltrated mail from the Albanian victim from October 2021 to January 2022. Mandiant lists the Albania operation among activity of clusters sharing tradecraft with UNC1860 but could not corroborate UNC1860's role.

campaigns.name: Destructive attack on Albanian government
campaigns.summary: Microsoft assessed with high confidence that Iranian government-sponsored actors, multiple in number, conducted the attack; DEV-0861 was credited with initial access and exfiltration phases.

campaigns.name: ShroudedSnooper reporting (Cisco Talos)
campaigns.summary: Talos reported a new intrusion set targeting Middle East telecom providers with HTTPSnoop and PipeSnoop backdoors, with no attribution to a known group. Mandiant later states Shrouded Snooper shares tradecraft and targeting with UNC1860.

campaigns.name: Scarred Manticore report (Check Point)
campaigns.summary: Check Point reported an MOIS-affiliated espionage campaign using LIONTAIL against Middle East government, military and telecom targets, with some tools tied to the Albania attack.

campaigns.name: BABYWIPER attacks in Israel (related clusters)
campaigns.summary: Mandiant reports these groups reportedly provided initial access for BABYWIPER attacks on Israel in late October 2023; it could not independently corroborate UNC1860's role.

campaigns.name: Israeli National Cyber Directorate wiper reporting
campaigns.summary: The INCD reported wiper activity against managed service providers, local governments and academia; indicators included the STAYSHANTE web shell and SASHEYAWAY dropper, which Mandiant attributes to UNC1860.

campaigns.name: Check Point on Void Manticore hand-off
campaigns.summary: Check Point reported victim overlap and systematic hand-off of targets from Scarred Manticore (initial access, data theft, CVE-2019-0604 in Israel) to Void Manticore, which deployed a wiper.

campaigns.name: Mandiant publishes UNC1860 'Temple of Oats' report
campaigns.summary: Mandiant details UNC1860's tooling, passive backdoors and probable initial-access-provider role, and releases YARA rules and a technical annex.

diamond.adversary: Iranian state-sponsored cluster, likely MOIS-affiliated, acting as an access provider for other actors including APT34 [S1].
diamond.capability: Web shells, GUI hand-off controllers, passive backdoors, and a repurposed kernel filter driver; SharePoint CVE-2019-0604 exploitation [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Passive implants with no outbound C2; commands may come from in-country VPN nodes, other victims or internal hosts; victim networks were used as staging in 2020 [S1].
diamond.victim: Government and telecommunications networks in the Middle East, with Iraq pivots noted [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Iranian state intelligence interest in regional government and telecom networks; related-cluster activity coincided with destructive operations against Albania and Israel [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing servers, notably unpatched SharePoint, and Windows hosts where kernel drivers can be loaded [S1][S2].

gaps: Mandiant could not corroborate UNC1860's role in the Albania (2022) and Israel (2023) destructive operations [S1].

The exact equivalence of UNC1860 with Shrouded Snooper, Scarred Manticore and Storm-0861 is not stated; Mandiant describes shared tradecraft and targeting only [S1]. Talos did not attribute ShroudedSnooper to a known group [S4].
Microsoft's Storm-0861 mapping is taken from the 2022 post's naming note; Microsoft's current actor-mapping file was not opened.
No post-September 2024 public reporting on UNC1860 was found in the searches run; current activity status is unknown.

Check Point's 2023 and 2024 reports and the Mandiant technical annex and IOC lists were read only through search summaries or the HTML post; the full primary text was not opened (Check Point host was unreachable).
No government (CISA, FBI, DOJ) attribution or advisory specific to UNC1860 was found.
Number and identity of victims, and which downstream actors used UNC1860 access beyond APT34, are not public in sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing SharePoint and other web servers in government and telecom networks are key terrain, as is any Windows host where an attacker can load a kernel driver [S1]. STEP 2: Passive implants with no outbound C2 and repurposed signed or legitimate drivers reduce the value of egress-based detection [S1]. STEP 3: The sourced template is opportunistic exploitation (for example CVE-2019-0604), web shell (STAYSHANTE), passive backdoor (TEMPLEDOOR, WINTAPIX), then hand-off over RDP via an HTTP proxy to a second actor [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued persistent access to Middle East government and telecom networks, with access passed to MOIS-affiliated espionage actors [S1]. MDCOA is that an inherited foothold is passed to a destructive actor, as Check Point describes for Scarred Manticore to Void Manticore and as Mandiant says is reported for Albania and Israel, so a foothold seen in espionage may precede a wiper event [S5][S1]. Candidate indicators: web shells under names mimicking Windows files in SharePoint LAYOUTS paths, unexpected kernel driver loads and filter-driver registrations, Event Log service stops and restarts, and inbound HTTPS requests to unusual URL patterns on servers [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: because UNC1860 is an access provider, treat any discovered UNC1860 tooling on a network as a sign that other actors may hold access, and widen scoping beyond the found implant [S1]. (2) Authorities: kernel-level and server forensics on partner or coalition networks need host-nation or owner consent and should be coordinated through the proper cyber authorities. (3) Mission assurance: patch status of internet-facing SharePoint and similar servers and driver-load monitoring on mission-critical Windows servers should be tracked for Middle East coalition and host-nation networks, given that related destructive operations followed intrusions in Albania and Israel [S1][S2]. (4) Coordination: share indicators (Mandiant YARA rules and hashes) with partners, and coordinate cross-vendor naming overlaps with the intelligence community rather than merging clusters in reporting [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: UNC1860 is a persistent and opportunistic Iranian state-sponsored threat actor that is likely affiliated with Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). A key feature of UNC1860 is its collection of specialized tooling and passive backdoors that Mandiant believes supports several objectives, including its role as a probable initial access provider and its ability to gain persistent access to high-priority networks, such as those in the government and telecommunications space throughout the Middle East.
